title: The Words Children Hear
text:
In the 1960s, Betty Hart and Todd Risley ran a preschool program in Kansas City and were frustrated that its vocabulary gains faded. They decided to look at what happened at home, long before preschool.

They recruited 42 families with babies, ranging from professional families to families receiving welfare. Every month for about two and a half years, from before the children could talk until they were three, an observer spent an hour in each home recording everything said to and around the child. The researchers then transcribed and coded the tapes, a task that took years.

The differences were striking. Some parents talked with their children far more than others, used a richer vocabulary, asked more questions and gave more encouragement and fewer prohibitions. On average, children in professional families heard many more words per hour than children in families on welfare. The amount and quality of talk in the home predicted the children's vocabulary at age three and their language skills in later school years.

Hart and Risley extrapolated that by age four, some children would have heard about 30 million fewer words than others, a figure that became famous as the word gap and shaped many parenting programs.
lesson: Talking with a small child, not just near them, is one of the simplest gifts you can give. Narrate, ask, listen and answer.
source: Hart, B., and Risley, T. R. (1995). Meaningful Differences in the Everyday Experience of Young American Children. Baltimore: Paul H. Brookes.
caveat: The sample was small, and later studies (for example Sperry, Sperry and Miller, 2019) have disputed the size of the class gap, especially when speech by other family members is counted.
